## Verdict

**C-14’s two conclusions follow from the cited results. I found no substantive gap in the posted deduction.** In particular, the proof handles the union over all admissible infinite itineraries, and its crucial identification of a tower parameter with the limit of the attachment points is justified.

There is one bibliographic qualification: I verified the required Cheraghi–Shishikura theorem in their manuscript, but could not confirm a refereed journal publication. The author’s bibliography and the arXiv record list the work without a journal reference. Thus the submission’s description as a deduction from “published results” should be made more precise. [arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/1509.07843?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

Here is my assessment of the mathematical assertions:

| Assertion | Assessment |
|---|---|
| The parameters with signed unit numerators and eventually \(q_{j+1}\ge q_j^2\) have planar Lebesgue measure zero. | Supported by the cited estimates and the covering argument. |
| The subfamily with eventually \(q_{j+1}=q_j^2\) has Hausdorff dimension zero. | Supported; the stronger conclusion survives inverse straightening. |

I checked the online proof, the relevant part of its accompanying note, and the cited source passages. The verification below is a reconstruction of the deduction from those source theorems; it is not a formal proof-assistant verification or a reproof of the entire source literature. The claim page itself currently labels the proof unverified. [Cairn Commons](https://cairn-commons.com/claims/C-14?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

## 1. The denominator condition really does imply Levin’s hypotheses

Choose a sufficiently late finite prefix of a tower and straighten its little Mandelbrot copy. In these normalized coordinates, write the remaining rotations as
\[
t_m=\frac{\varepsilon_m}{d_m},
\qquad \varepsilon_m\in\{-1,1\},
\]
and the parent periods as
\[
\nu_0=1,\qquad \nu_{m+1}=\nu_m d_m.
\]

We can choose the prefix after the growth condition begins, so that
\[
d_{m+1}\ge d_m^2\qquad(m\ge0).
\]
The starting denominator \(d_0\) can also be made as large as required: repeated squaring forces the denominators to diverge.

The decisive calculation is
\[
\frac{\nu_{m+1}}{d_{m+1}}
=
\frac{\nu_m d_m}{d_{m+1}}
\le
\frac{\nu_m}{d_m}.
\]
Induction gives
\[
\frac{\nu_m}{d_m}\le\frac1{d_0},
\]
and hence
\[
\nu_m|t_m|\le\frac1{d_0}.
\]

Levin’s Addendum, Lemma 0.5(C1), requires all denominators to exceed a fixed threshold
\[
Q=\max\{Q_0,Q_1\},
\]
together with
\[
|t_0|<\frac{\alpha}{8\pi},
\qquad
|t_m|<\frac{\alpha}{8\pi\nu_m}\quad(m\ge1).
\]
These are exactly the inequalities obtained by taking \(d_0>Q\) and \(1/d_0<\alpha/(8\pi)\). See PDF page 47 of the combined preprint. [arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0710.4406?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

This checks an essential point: the hypothesis involving **successive denominators** is sufficient for the small-angle estimates involving the **full normalized parent period**. No extra growth assumption is needed for this step.

The signs cause no difficulty because the relevant inequalities use \(|t_m|\). The convention that rotations lie in \((-1/2,1/2]\) also causes no problem once the denominators are sufficiently large.

## 2. Levin supplies the required uniform, finite-prefix neighborhoods

In Claim 1 of the proof of Lemma 0.5, Levin constructs nested sets
\[
R_m=\psi_m(B_m),
\qquad
B_m=B\!\left(0,\frac{\alpha}{2\nu_m}\right)
\quad(m\ge1),
\]
with
\[
|\psi_m'|\le C_0\frac{2^m}{\nu_m^2}.
\]
Consequently, for a fixed constant \(C_L\),
\[
\operatorname{diam}R_m
\le C_L\frac{2^m}{\nu_m^3}. \tag{1}
\]
The marked attachment point at level \(m\) belongs to \(R_m\), and \(R_{m+1}\subset R_m\). These are Claim 1(i)–(iii), on PDF pages 48–49. [arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0710.4406?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

Two details matter for using these sets as a cover.

**The constant is uniform over itineraries.** The starting map is the inverse log-multiplier map for the main cardioid,
\[
\psi_0(L)=\frac{e^L}{2}-\frac{e^{2L}}4.
\]
Its derivative is bounded on the fixed starting disk. Thus the initial constant does not vary with the later rotation choices.

**The indexing is suitable for a finite-prefix cover.** The component of period \(\nu_m\), its multiplier map, and the disk \(B_m\) are determined by
\[
t_0,\ldots,t_{m-1}.
\]
So \(R_m\) depends on those first \(m\) rotations. The next rotation \(t_m\) selects the next attachment point inside that already determined neighborhood.

Let \(a_m\) denote these attachment points. For every \(k\ge m\),
\[
a_k\in R_k\subset R_m.
\]
Since \(\nu_m\ge2^m\), equation (1) implies that the diameters tend to zero. The attachment points therefore have a common limit \(a_\infty\), and
\[
a_\infty\in\overline{R_m}\qquad\text{for every }m.
\]
Taking closures does not increase the diameters.

At this stage, however, one still has to prove that an arbitrary parameter with this itinerary is \(a_\infty\). That is the next step.

## 3. Cheraghi–Shishikura closes the parameter-inclusion step

This is the most consequential part of the verification.

Let
\[
K_m=M(t_0,\ldots,t_{m-1})
\]
be the finite-prefix parameter locus for the normalized itinerary. Cheraghi–Shishikura’s **Theorem D**, on manuscript page 6, gives uniform constants \(N,C_R\) and \(0<\lambda<1\) such that
\[
\operatorname{diam}K_m\le C_R\lambda^m. \tag{2}
\]
The example immediately following the theorem explicitly includes signed unit numerators, an initial denominator at least \(N\), and successive denominators satisfying \(d_{m+1}\ge d_m^2\). Exact squaring is included. [ma.imperial.ac.uk](https://www.ma.imperial.ac.uk/~dcheragh/Research/2015-2.pdf?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

The remaining question is whether these loci are the same objects needed in C-14. They are: §4.3, manuscript pages 48–49, identifies them with the nested satellite Mandelbrot copies obtained by successive inverse straightenings. It also places each root in the corresponding copy. [ma.imperial.ac.uk](https://www.ma.imperial.ac.uk/~dcheragh/Research/2015-2.pdf?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

Now take any parameter \(c\) realizing the infinite itinerary. For each fixed \(m\),
\[
c\in K_m.
\]
Every sufficiently late attachment point \(a_k\) also belongs to \(K_m\), by nesting. If one uses a convention that omits an exceptional parabolic root from a renormalizable locus, the same assertion holds in its closure, with unchanged diameter.

It follows from (2) that
\[
|c-a_k|\le C_R\lambda^m
\]
for all sufficiently large \(k\). Passing to the attachment-point limit gives
\[
|c-a_\infty|\le C_R\lambda^m.
\]
Since this holds for every \(m\),
\[
c=a_\infty.
\]
Therefore
\[
c\in\overline{R_m}\qquad\text{for every }m. \tag{3}
\]

Equation (3) is the inclusion the later covering argument needs.

### Why using rigidity here is essential

Levin’s separate whole-limb inclusion has the stronger hypothesis
\[
\frac{d_m}{\nu_m^2}>\frac8\alpha.
\]
It is not a consequence of the condition in C-14. [arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0710.4406?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

For example, under exact squaring,
\[
d_m=d_0^{2^m},
\qquad
\nu_m=d_0^{2^m-1},
\]
so
\[
\frac{d_m}{\nu_m^2}
=
d_0^{\,2-2^m}\longrightarrow0.
\]
Thus an argument that simply applied whole-limb inclusion would fail for an explicitly claimed subfamily. C-14 avoids that problem by using the shrinking finite-prefix loci to identify the parameter with the attachment-point limit. The cited theorem supports that use.

Uniqueness for each itinerary does not by itself give a measure-zero set: an uncountable union of singletons can have positive area. The covering argument must control all possible continuations together.

Here is an explicit version of that argument.

Fix \(s>1/3\). Since \(3s>1\), choose an integer \(Q_s\) sufficiently large that
\[
\theta_s
=
2^{s+1}\sum_{q\ge Q_s}q^{-3s}
<1. \tag{4}
\]

Every admissible itinerary eventually has all denominators at least \(Q_s\). Partition the family according to a finite prefix \(w\) after which that is true. There are only countably many such prefixes.

**Keep the same normalized parameter coordinates throughout this partition.** No additional straightening is needed when introducing \(Q_s\).

Suppose \(w\) has length \(k\), and define
\[
D_w=C_L\frac{2^k}{\nu_k^3}.
\]
For a continuation with \(\ell\) further rotations, equation (1) gives
\[
\operatorname{diam}R_{k+\ell}
\le
D_w\prod_{j=k}^{k+\ell-1}\frac2{d_j^3}. \tag{5}
\]

\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{\text{admissible continuations}}
\bigl(\operatorname{diam}\overline{R_{k+\ell}}\bigr)^s
&\le
D_w^s
\left(
\sum_{q\ge Q_s}2\left(\frac2{q^3}\right)^s
\right)^\ell\\
&=
D_w^s\theta_s^\ell
\longrightarrow0.
\end{aligned}
\tag{6}
\]

This estimate deliberately sums over more denominator choices than the growth condition allows. That is legitimate for an upper bound.

The largest covering diameter also tends to zero:
\[
\sup\operatorname{diam}\overline{R_{k+\ell}}
\le
D_w\left(\frac2{Q_s^3}\right)^\ell
\longrightarrow0. \tag{7}
\]

Equations (3), (6), and (7) show that the subfamily with prefix \(w\) has zero \(s\)-dimensional Hausdorff measure. Taking the countable union over \(w\) preserves this conclusion.

Since this works for every \(s>1/3\), the normalized family \(E\) satisfies
\[
\boxed{\dim_H E\le\frac13.}
\]
In particular, it has planar Lebesgue measure zero.

There is no quantifier problem in allowing \(Q_s\), and hence the prefix partition, to depend on \(s\). Hausdorff dimension is established by proving the required vanishing separately for each \(s>1/3\).

## 5. Exact squaring gives Hausdorff dimension zero

Now fix \(d_0\) and impose
\[
d_{m+1}=d_m^2
\qquad(m\ge0).
\]
Then
\[
d_m=d_0^{2^m},
\]
and
\[
\nu_m
=
\prod_{j=0}^{m-1}d_j
=
d_0^{1+2+\cdots+2^{m-1}}
=
d_0^{2^m-1}.
\]

Only the signs remain free. At level \(m\), there are at most \(2^m\) prefixes. By equation (1), each is covered by a set of diameter at most
\[
C_L2^m d_0^{-3(2^m-1)}.
\]

For any \(s>0\), the total \(s\)-cost of this cover is therefore bounded by
\[
2^m
\left[
C_L2^m d_0^{-3(2^m-1)}
\right]^s
=
C_L^s2^{m(1+s)}
d_0^{-3s(2^m-1)}. \tag{8}
\]
Its logarithm is
\[
s\log C_L
+
m(1+s)\log2
-
3s(2^m-1)\log d_0,
\]
which tends to \(-\infty\). Thus (8) tends to zero for **every** \(s>0\), and the maximum covering diameter also tends to zero.

This proves dimension zero for each fixed starting denominator. Taking the countable union over starting denominators preserves dimension zero.

The reason the stronger conclusion works is precise: the number of sign prefixes grows exponentially in \(m\), while the diameters decrease at a rate involving \(d_0^{-3\cdot2^m}\). The latter dominates for every positive Hausdorff exponent.

The estimates above apply in normalized coordinates. To obtain the original claim, one must return to each original little copy.

Write its canonical straightening as
\[
\chi_T:T\longrightarrow M,
\]
and its inverse as \(h_T=\chi_T^{-1}\).

Lyubich’s **Theorem 5.5 and the following remark**, journal page 366, provide quasiconformal extensions of this correspondence for primitive copies, and locally away from the root for satellite copies. The discussion preceding the theorem identifies the correspondence as the canonical straightening map. [emis.de](https://www.emis.de/ft/50722?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

This interpretation is also explicitly confirmed in Lomonaco–Petersen’s account of Lyubich’s result: the Douady–Hubbard homeomorphism has the required quasiconformal regularity outside arbitrarily small neighborhoods of a satellite root. - **Planar nullity:** a planar quasiconformal map sends sets of area zero to sets of area zero—Lusin’s property \(N\).
- **Dimension zero:** a quasiconformal map is locally Hölder continuous with a positive exponent.

Both properties hold for the inverse maps as well. Astala’s area-distortion theorem supplies the null-set preservation, and the same paper records local \(1/K\)-Hölder continuity for \(K\)-quasiconformal maps. For the dimension assertion, the relevant elementary consequence is that an \(\eta\)-Hölder map satisfies
\[
\dim_H h(A)\le\frac{\dim_H A}{\eta}.
\]
If \(\dim_H A=0\), its image therefore also has dimension zero.

For a satellite copy, exhaust the copy away from its root by compact sets. Each compact set is covered by finitely many suitable local charts. Apply the relevant property in each chart, then take the countable union and add the root singleton.

No uniform distortion constant or Hölder exponent is needed across this exhaustion:

- Every chart sends an area-null set to an area-null set.
- Every positive Hölder exponent sends a dimension-zero set to a dimension-zero set.

\[
f_c^{\,n}(0)=0,
\]
which has finitely many solutions. Countable unions preserve both conclusions.

\[

\qquad
\dim_H(S_=)=0.

\]
